title: Lecture Notes
text:
2 Presence and Immersion

2.1 Defining Presence
Presence is one of the most studied and debated concepts in XR research. At its simplest, it is the feeling of “being there” — the sense that you are actually in the virtual environment rather than observing it from outside.
Mel Slater, one of the leading researchers in this area, distinguishes two components of presence:
Place Illusion (PI) is the strong illusion of being in a place even though you know you are not. It is supported primarily by the quality of the sensorimotor contingencies — the relationship between your movements and the changes in the sensory display. If you turn your head and the visual scene updates correctly, your brain interprets this as evidence that you are in a real place.
Plausibility Illusion (Psi) is the illusion that what is happening is really happening. It is supported by the responsiveness of the environment — if you reach out and touch a virtual object and it responds, your brain interprets this as evidence that the event is real.
Slater argues that both PI and Psi are necessary for full presence. A highly immersive display that shows a completely unresponsive environment will produce PI but not Psi. A responsive environment on a low-quality display may produce Psi but not PI.


2.2 Immersion as an Objective Property
Immersion is often used interchangeably with presence, but they are distinct. Immersion is an objective, measurable property of the technology — it describes how completely the system replaces the user’s sensory input with synthetic input.
A system with a wide FOV, high resolution, low latency, and spatial audio is more immersive than one with a narrow FOV and no audio. But a user may feel more present in the less immersive system if the content is more compelling and responsive.
This distinction has important design implications. You cannot guarantee presence by maximising immersion. You must also design content that supports plausibility.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
3 Perceptual Modalities
The brain integrates information from multiple sensory systems simultaneously. In XR, understanding each modality helps you design experiences that support presence and avoid discomfort.

3.1 Visual Perception
Vision is the dominant sense in most XR systems. The visual system provides information about:
Stereopsis: The brain uses the slight difference in the images received by each eye (binocular disparity) to compute depth. HMDs present slightly different images to each eye to simulate this. The effectiveness of stereopsis depends on the accuracy of the interpupillary distance (IPD) setting.
Motion parallax: As you move your head, objects at different distances move at different rates across your visual field. This is a powerful depth cue that is well-supported by 6DOF tracking.
Accommodation and vergence: As discussed in Week 2, the vergence-accommodation conflict is a significant limitation of current HMDs.
Peripheral vision: The peripheral visual field is important for detecting motion and maintaining spatial awareness. A narrow FOV that cuts off peripheral vision reduces immersion and can cause disorientation.


3.2 Auditory Perception
The auditory system contributes significantly to presence. Research has shown that high-quality spatial audio can increase presence scores substantially, and that audio that does not match the visual scene can break presence rapidly.
The brain localises sounds using:
Interaural Time Difference (ITD): The difference in the time it takes for a sound to reach each ear. Sounds from the left arrive at the left ear slightly before the right ear.
Interaural Level Difference (ILD): The difference in the loudness of a sound at each ear. The head creates an acoustic shadow that attenuates sounds on the far side.
Spectral cues: The shape of the outer ear (pinna) modifies the frequency content of sounds in ways that depend on the direction of the source. These spectral cues are captured in the HRTF and are particularly important for distinguishing sounds above and below the listener.


3.3 Proprioception
Proprioception is the sense of the position and movement of your own body, provided by receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints. It tells you where your limbs are without looking at them.
In VR, proprioception can conflict with visual information. If you see your virtual hand in a position that does not match where your real hand is, this creates a conflict that can be disorienting. This is why accurate hand tracking and controller tracking are important for natural interaction.


3.4 The Vestibular System
The vestibular system, located in the inner ear, detects:

linear acceleration (moving forward, backward, up, down)
rotational acceleration (turning)
the direction of gravity

The vestibular system is the primary cause of simulator sickness in VR. When the visual system detects motion (because the virtual environment is moving) but the vestibular system detects no motion (because the user is stationary), the brain interprets this conflict as a sign of poisoning — a response that evolved to protect against neurotoxins that cause hallucinations. The result is nausea.
This is called vection — the perception of self-motion induced by visual stimulation alone.


3.5 Haptic Perception
The haptic system encompasses touch (cutaneous sensation) and force (kinaesthetic sensation). It provides information about:

surface texture
temperature
compliance (how much an object deforms under pressure)
weight and inertia

Current XR systems provide very limited haptic feedback — primarily vibration from controller motors. The absence of rich haptic feedback is a significant limitation for experiences that involve object manipulation, surface interaction, or social presence (the feeling of being with another person).

title: Lecture Notes
text:
4 Proximal and Distal Stimuli
This distinction, drawn from perceptual psychology, is useful for understanding how XR works.
The distal stimulus is the actual object or event in the world — a tree, a voice, a surface.
The proximal stimulus is the pattern of energy that reaches the sensory receptor — the pattern of light on the retina, the pressure wave at the eardrum, the pressure on the skin.
The brain never has direct access to the distal stimulus. It only has access to the proximal stimulus, and it must infer the distal stimulus from that. This inference is based on prior experience, context, and the integration of multiple sensory signals.
XR works by manipulating the proximal stimulus. We cannot put a real tree in front of the user, but we can create a pattern of light on the retina that is consistent with the presence of a tree. If the proximal stimulus is convincing enough, the brain will infer the presence of the tree — and the user will feel present in a forest.
This framing helps explain why presence is not simply a function of display quality. The brain is not just checking whether the image is photorealistic. It is checking whether the pattern of sensory input is consistent with being in a real place. Consistency across modalities, responsiveness to movement, and plausible cause-and-effect relationships are all important.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
5 Simulator Sickness

5.1 Definition and Symptoms
Simulator sickness is a form of motion sickness that occurs in simulated environments. Symptoms include:

nausea and stomach discomfort
disorientation and dizziness
eye strain and headache
fatigue
pallor and sweating in severe cases

Symptoms typically develop during or after use and can persist for some time after the headset is removed.


5.2 Causes
Latency is the delay between the user’s head movement and the corresponding update of the display. Even small amounts of latency (above approximately 20 milliseconds) can cause discomfort. Modern HMDs use asynchronous timewarp and reprojection techniques to minimise perceived latency.
Low frame rate causes judder — a stuttering of the image during movement. This is both visually unpleasant and a significant cause of sickness. Maintaining a consistent frame rate above 72Hz is essential.
Vection — visual motion without vestibular motion — is the primary cause of sickness during smooth locomotion in VR. The visual system detects movement, but the vestibular system does not, creating a conflict.
FOV mismatch occurs when the visual motion in the display does not match the expected motion for the user’s real-world movement. This can occur with incorrect camera settings or locomotion implementations.


5.3 Mitigation Strategies
Teleportation eliminates vection by moving the user instantaneously rather than continuously. It is the most effective comfort option for locomotion.
Vignetting reduces the peripheral visual field during movement, which reduces the vection signal. Many VR games offer this as a comfort option.
Snap turning rotates the user’s view in discrete steps rather than continuously, eliminating rotational vection.
Frame rate maintenance is critical. Dropping below the target frame rate is more disorienting than a consistently lower frame rate.
User control — allowing users to choose their preferred locomotion method and comfort settings — is important because susceptibility to simulator sickness varies significantly between individuals.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
6 Health Effects and Ethics

6.1 Physical Health Effects
Beyond simulator sickness, extended XR use can cause:

Eye strain and fatigue from the vergence-accommodation conflict and sustained focus at a fixed distance
Neck and shoulder strain from the weight of the headset and sustained head positions
Post-VR disorientation — a brief period of disorientation after removing the headset, particularly after extended use
Social isolation — extended use of fully immersive VR removes the user from their physical social environment



6.2 Ethical Responsibilities
The power of presence creates ethical responsibilities for XR designers.
Disclosure: Users should be informed of potential health risks before using XR systems, particularly for extended sessions.
Comfort options: Experiences should provide comfort options (teleportation, vignetting, session time limits) rather than forcing users into uncomfortable configurations.
Accessibility: XR experiences should be designed to be accessible to users with different physical abilities, sensory sensitivities, and susceptibilities to simulator sickness.
Manipulation: The sense of presence can be exploited to create powerful emotional responses. This raises questions about the ethics of using XR for persuasion, advertising, or behaviour change. Designers should consider whether their use of presence is in the user’s interest.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
7 Measuring Presence
Several standardised questionnaires have been developed to measure presence:
The Presence Questionnaire (PQ) (Witmer and Singer, 1998) measures presence across several dimensions including involvement, sensory fidelity, and interface quality.
The Igroup Presence Questionnaire (IPQ) (Schubert et al., 2001) measures spatial presence, involvement, and realness.
These tools are useful for comparing different design decisions and for evaluating the effectiveness of XR experiences. You will use them in Week 11 when we cover evaluation methods.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
This module sits at the intersection of technology, design, and human experience. By the time you finish it, you should be able to think critically about immersive systems, build functional XR prototypes, and evaluate them against established principles of human-computer interaction.
This first week establishes the conceptual landscape. Before we can design or build anything, we need a shared vocabulary and a clear understanding of what XR actually is, where it came from, and where it is going.
It is worth being honest about why the vocabulary matters, because “getting the definitions right” can look like an academic exercise. It is not. The terms in this lecture map directly onto engineering decisions. Whether a system is optical see-through or video see-through determines what your content can look like, because you cannot render black on an optical display. Whether tracking is 3DOF or 6DOF determines whether a user can lean around an object, which in turn determines whether your scene can contain anything worth leaning around. Whether a device understands the room it is in determines whether your content can sit on a real table or must float in front of the user’s face. Every one of these is a design constraint before it is a technical specification, and the words we use are how we reason about them.
A second point before we begin. This field has an unusually strong marketing vocabulary running alongside its technical one, and the two frequently disagree. Manufacturers describe their products in whatever terms are currently favourable — the same headset has been sold as VR, as mixed reality, and as spatial computing within a few years, without the hardware changing much. Part of your job on this module is to be able to look past the positioning and describe what a device actually does. The hype cycle section below gives you a framework for doing exactly that.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
2 Defining the XR Spectrum
The term XR (Extended Reality) is an umbrella that covers several related but distinct technologies. Understanding the differences between them is essential because each imposes different design constraints and affords different possibilities.

2.1 Virtual Reality (VR)
In a VR system, the user’s visual field is entirely replaced by a synthetic environment. The headset blocks out the physical world and presents a stereoscopic 3D image that responds to the user’s head movement. High-quality VR systems also include spatial audio, hand controllers with haptic feedback, and room-scale tracking.
The defining characteristic of VR is sensory substitution — the system replaces real sensory input with synthetic input. The quality of this substitution determines how convincing the experience feels.
Two consequences follow from total visual replacement, and they shape almost everything in the rest of this module.
The first is that the system becomes responsible for the user’s safety. Someone in a VR headset cannot see the floor, the furniture, other people, or their own hands unless you draw them. This is why guardian and boundary systems exist, and why every lab session in this module begins by clearing a floor area. It is also why a VR experience that encourages large physical movement carries a duty of care that a screen-based one does not.
The second is that the system becomes responsible for the user’s comfort in a way no screen is. If the image lags behind head movement, the user’s visual system reports one thing and their vestibular system reports another, and the result is nausea. We return to this properly in Week 3, but note now that this is a physiological response to a technical failure — not a matter of the user being sensitive or insufficiently accustomed.


2.2 Augmented Reality (AR)
AR systems overlay digital content onto the user’s view of the real world. This can be achieved through:

optical see-through displays (the user looks through a transparent lens with digital content projected onto it — HoloLens 2, Snap Spectacles)
video see-through displays (cameras capture the real world and the combined image is displayed — Quest 3 passthrough, mobile AR)
projection-based AR (digital content is projected directly onto real surfaces)

The defining characteristic of AR is that the real world remains visible and the digital content must be registered accurately to physical space.
That word registered is doing a great deal of work. Registration means the digital content holds its correct position relative to the physical world as the user moves. A virtual object that slides a few centimetres when you turn your head is not augmenting reality; it is floating in front of your eyes. Registration quality is the single clearest technical difference between a convincing AR system and an unconvincing one, and it is why Week 7 spends an entire session on spatial mapping and anchors.
The distinction between optical and video see-through has consequences that catch people out repeatedly, so it is worth stating plainly:

You cannot render black on an optical see-through display. These displays add light to the scene; they cannot subtract it. Black is simply the absence of projected light, which means it is transparent. Dark UI, drop shadows and solid backgrounds all fail. Content must be designed to read as luminous.
Video see-through can render black, but everything you see is a camera image. Real-world colour, dynamic range and latency are all mediated by the camera pipeline. The real world is subject to the same frame budget as your content.
Occlusion works differently in each. On a video see-through system, you can composite virtual objects behind real ones if you have depth data. On most optical systems, virtual content is additive light and will appear to ghost through real objects regardless.



2.3 Mixed Reality (MR)
Mixed reality is a term used in different ways by different organisations. In its most precise sense (following Milgram and Kishino’s taxonomy), MR refers to any point on the reality-virtuality continuum between fully real and fully virtual. In practice, it is often used to describe systems where digital and physical objects interact — for example, a virtual ball that bounces off a real table.
The HoloLens 2 and Meta Quest 3 are both marketed as mixed reality devices.
The looseness of this term is worth naming rather than resolving. In current industry usage, “mixed reality” most often signals that a headset can show you the real world through passthrough and place content in it with some awareness of geometry. That is a meaningful capability, but it is a narrower claim than Milgram’s, and when you read a specification sheet you should establish which sense is meant. The practical test is to ask what the system knows about the room: a device that merely shows you a camera feed is doing something quite different from one that has detected your walls, floor and furniture and can place a virtual object on your actual desk.


2.4 Spatial Computing
Spatial computing is a broader paradigm that describes computing systems that understand and interact with three-dimensional space. Rather than confining computation to a screen, spatial computing embeds it in the environment. This includes XR devices but also extends to robotics, autonomous vehicles, and smart environments.
Apple’s Vision Pro is positioned explicitly as a spatial computing device rather than a VR or AR headset, reflecting a deliberate shift in how the industry frames these technologies.
The framing shift is not only marketing. It carries a real claim: that the interesting property of these systems is not the display but the spatial awareness — the device’s model of where it is, what is around it, and how the user relates to both. On that reading, a headset is one form factor among several, and the defining capability is persistence. Content that knows where it is, and is still there tomorrow, behaves like part of the environment rather than like an application you launched.
This is the sense in which the module title uses the term, and it is why the second half of the semester moves from interaction technique into mapping, anchoring and environment design.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
3 The Reality-Virtuality Continuum
Milgram and Kishino (1994) proposed a taxonomy of mixed reality visual displays that remains influential today. They described a continuum from fully real environments to fully virtual environments, with augmented reality and augmented virtuality occupying the middle ground.









Real Environment
Augmented Reality
Augmented Virtuality
Virtual Environment




Fully real
Mostly real, some virtual
Mostly virtual, some real
Fully virtual



This framework is useful because it reminds us that the distinction between VR and AR is not binary. Many modern devices can operate at different points on this continuum depending on their mode of use.
Augmented virtuality is the least familiar of these terms and the most useful for understanding modern hardware. It describes a predominantly virtual environment into which real elements are imported — a virtual meeting room containing a live video feed of a real colleague, or a fully synthetic scene in which your real hands are visible. A Quest 3 running a VR application that shows your real keyboard through passthrough is operating in augmented virtuality, and this is now a common design pattern rather than an exotic one.
Two cautions about applying the taxonomy.
First, it is a taxonomy of visual displays, published in 1994 and framed accordingly. It says nothing about audio, haptics, interaction technique or social presence, all of which matter as much as the visual channel and some of which we will argue matter more. When you position an experience on the continuum in Week 6, you are describing one dimension of it.
Second, modern devices move along the continuum at runtime. A single Quest 3 application may open in passthrough, fade to a fully virtual environment for a task, and return. The useful question is therefore not “where does this device sit” but “where does this experience sit, at this moment, and why did the designer choose that point?” That question is the basis of the analysis you will produce for Assessment 2.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
4 A Brief History of XR
Understanding the history of XR helps contextualise the current moment and avoid repeating past mistakes.

4.1 Early Foundations (1960s–1990s)

1965: Ivan Sutherland describes the “Ultimate Display” — a room in which the computer can control the existence of matter
1968: Sutherland builds the first HMD, the Sword of Damocles
1987: Jaron Lanier coins the term “virtual reality”
1992: The CAVE (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment) is developed at the University of Illinois
1994: Milgram and Kishino publish their taxonomy of mixed reality

Sutherland’s 1965 essay is worth reading in full — it is three pages long and remarkably undated. His formulation of the goal, a display in which matter itself can be controlled by the computer, still describes the ambition better than most contemporary marketing. The 1968 headset that followed was so heavy it had to be suspended from the ceiling, which is where its nickname comes from.
The early 1990s produced the field’s first consumer wave, and its first collapse. Virtuality arcade machines appeared in shopping centres, Sega announced and then cancelled a headset, and Nintendo shipped the Virtual Boy in 1995 to poor sales and widespread complaints of headaches. The technology could not yet deliver what the concept promised: displays were low resolution, tracking was slow, and latency was high enough to make many users unwell within minutes. The lesson is not that the ideas were wrong but that immersive systems fail ungracefully. A screen application that runs poorly is annoying; an immersive one that runs poorly makes people ill and they do not come back.


4.2 The First Consumer Wave (2012–2016)

2012: Oculus Rift Kickstarter campaign raises $2.4 million
2014: Facebook acquires Oculus for $2 billion
2016: Consumer launches of Oculus Rift, HTC Vive, and PlayStation VR
2016: Pokémon GO demonstrates mass-market AR

What changed between 1995 and 2012 was largely borrowed rather than invented. The smartphone industry had driven down the cost of high-density displays, accelerometers, gyroscopes and mobile processors to the point where a headset could be assembled from commodity parts. This is a recurring pattern in the field and a useful lens for evaluating claims about the future: ask which adjacent industry is paying for the component improvements.
Pokémon GO deserves particular attention because it is the most commercially successful AR product to date and it uses almost none of the technology this module covers. There was no registration to speak of, no depth sensing, no scene understanding. Its achievement was locational and social rather than perceptual, which is a useful corrective to the assumption that technical sophistication drives adoption.


4.3 Standalone and Spatial Computing (2019–present)

2019: Meta Quest 1 launches — standalone VR without a PC
2021: Meta rebrands from Facebook, announces metaverse strategy
2022: Meta Quest Pro introduces mixed reality passthrough
2023: Apple announces Vision Pro at WWDC
2024: Spatial computing enters enterprise and consumer markets at scale

The significant transition here is the removal of the cable. Standalone headsets traded graphical fidelity for the elimination of a PC, a setup process and a tether, and that trade turned out to be strongly favourable for adoption. It also created the constraint you will spend Week 10 working within: a standalone headset is a mobile device with a mobile GPU, rendering two views at 72Hz or better, and your frame budget is correspondingly tight.
The current period is best understood as unresolved rather than settled. Headsets are capable but bulky; glasses are comfortable but limited; the compelling consumer application has not obviously arrived; and enterprise deployment is growing steadily but with less visibility. You are studying this field during a genuinely open moment, which is more interesting than studying a mature one.

title: Lecture Notes
section: 5 Ten Years of Hype: Reading Expectations Against Reality
text:
5 Ten Years of Hype: Reading Expectations Against Reality
The timeline above tells you what happened. It does not tell you what people expected to happen at each point, and the gap between the two is where most of the field’s bad decisions — and a fair amount of good research funding — have come from. To read that gap, we can use Gartner’s Hype Cycle, a model of how expectations for an emerging technology tend to change over time, independently of how the underlying technology is actually progressing.

5.1 The Hype Cycle Model
Gartner’s model describes five phases that a technology typically passes through in the public and industry imagination:

Innovation Trigger — a breakthrough, product launch or demonstration generates significant press interest
Peak of Inflated Expectations — early publicity produces a number of success stories, often accompanied by scores of failures; expectations run well ahead of demonstrated capability
Trough of Disillusionment — interest wanes as experiments and implementations fail to deliver; producers of the technology shake out or fail
Slope of Enlightenment — more instances of how the technology can benefit the enterprise or consumer start to crystallise and become more widely understood
Plateau of Productivity — mainstream adoption starts to take off; the technology’s broad market applicability and relevance are paying off

Before applying this to XR, it is worth being honest about what the model is and is not. It is a communication tool, not a measuring instrument — Gartner does not disclose a rigorous methodology for placing a technology at a specific point, and the chart has been criticised for being unfalsifiable, since almost any subsequent event can be narrated as fitting one phase or another. Treat what follows as a structured way of organising a history you already partly know, not as evidence of a natural law that immersive technologies must obey.


5.2 Virtual Reality: 2015 → 2018
VR entered its innovation trigger around the Oculus Kickstarter and the Facebook acquisition, climbed rapidly to a peak of inflated expectations around the 2016 consumer launches (Rift, Vive, PSVR), and then slid into a trough of disillusionment as consumer sales underwhelmed, content libraries remained thin, and the promised killer application did not arrive. The technology did not get worse during this period — if anything, standalone headsets were already in development — but the expectation collapsed faster than the hardware improved.


5.3 Augmented Reality: 2016 → 2019
AR followed a similar but offset arc, triggered by Pokémon GO’s runaway 2016 success and ARKit/ARCore’s 2017 launches, which briefly promised AR as the next mobile computing platform. Expectations peaked around 2017–2018 and then fell as it became clear that phone-based AR, without registration or persistence beyond a single session, was a novelty layer rather than a platform shift for most consumer use cases.


5.4 The Metaverse Spike: 2022 → 2023
The metaverse spike is the sharpest and most recent example in the chart, and the most useful one for you to study critically. Meta’s 2021 rebrand and subsequent investment triggered an intense peak of inflated expectations through 2022, with enormous capital committed to virtual real estate, corporate presence and social VR platforms. By 2023, user numbers, engagement figures and press sentiment had all fallen sharply, and much of that investment was quietly written down or redirected. Note what this spike measures: it says very little about whether headset hardware improved in that period (it did — Quest 3 launched in the middle of the trough), and a great deal about how a marketing narrative outran what the technology could support.


5.5 Spatial Computing: 2024 → 2025
The current reframing around “spatial computing”, prompted substantially by Apple’s Vision Pro announcement and launch, shows the early shape of a new innovation trigger and peak. It is deliberately positioned as distinct from the exhausted “VR” and “metaverse” branding, which is itself a useful data point: when a term becomes commercially damaged, the industry does not usually fix the underlying problem, it renames the category. Whether spatial computing repeats the same arc, plateaus faster because the underlying hardware and software ecosystem is more mature, or fails to trigger a peak at all, is an open question you are positioned to watch unfold during this module rather than read about after the fact.


5.6 Ten Years, One Chart
Plotted together, VR, AR, the metaverse and spatial computing do not form one clean curve — they form four overlapping cycles at different phases, which is closer to how the field actually behaves than any single narrative of “XR” as one technology on one trajectory. Some of these labels describe genuinely different capabilities; some describe the same underlying hardware rebranded to escape a damaged reputation. Distinguishing the two is a skill, not a fact you can look up.


5.7 What Leaving the Cycle Means
The most useful lesson from ten years of this chart is not where any single label currently sits, but what happens to a technology that survives its trough. A technology that reaches the plateau of productivity typically stops being discussed as a hype phenomenon at all — it simply becomes infrastructure. Nobody today writes hype-cycle commentary about the smartphone touchscreen or GPS. If spatial computing succeeds, the marker of that success will not be a triumphant peak; it will be the field’s vocabulary quietly disappearing from the technology press because the capability has become unremarkable. Judge claims about “where XR is heading” against that standard: a technology that is still being sold on its promise, rather than used without comment, has not yet reached the plateau, whatever the marketing implies.


5.8 Discussion: Hype and Evidence
Carry these questions with you through the rest of the module, and revisit them explicitly when you scope Assessment 2 and 3:

If expectations collapsed for the metaverse while the hardware (Quest 3, passthrough mixed reality) kept improving, what was the hype cycle chart actually measuring — the technology, or the narrative around it?
Is “spatial computing” a genuinely distinct technical paradigm from VR/AR/MR, or a rebranding exercise timed to distance the industry from the metaverse trough? What evidence would distinguish the two?
When you evaluate a piece of hardware or a research claim later in this module, how will you separate its demonstrated capability from the phase of the hype cycle its category currently occupies?

title: Lecture Notes
text:
6 Degrees of Freedom
A fundamental concept in XR hardware is degrees of freedom (DOF), which describes how many independent axes of movement a tracking system can detect.

6.1 3DOF
Three degrees of freedom tracks rotation only:

pitch (nodding)
yaw (shaking head)
roll (tilting head)

3DOF systems cannot detect the user moving through space. They are suitable for 360-degree video viewing but not for interactive VR.
The perceptual consequence is worth experiencing rather than reading about. In a 3DOF system, leaning to look around an object does not work — the world rotates with you but does not shift, so the object stays stubbornly in front of you. Because your vestibular system correctly reports that you moved while your eyes report that the world did not respond, 3DOF systems tend to feel subtly wrong even to users who cannot articulate why, and they provoke discomfort more readily than 6DOF systems during any movement more energetic than sitting still.


6.2 6DOF
Six degrees of freedom tracks rotation and position:

pitch, yaw, roll (rotation)
x, y, z (position in space)

6DOF allows the user to physically move through the virtual environment. All primary devices in this module support 6DOF tracking.
6DOF is what makes parallax work, and parallax is a large part of why virtual objects read as solid and located rather than as images. It is also what makes physical crouching, leaning and stepping available as interaction techniques — a design vocabulary with no screen-based equivalent.
Note that head tracking and controller tracking are separate questions. A headset may be 6DOF while its controllers are 3DOF, which was common in earlier standalone devices and immediately rules out direct manipulation of objects in space.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
7 Tracking Technologies

7.1 Inside-Out Tracking
Cameras mounted on the headset observe the environment and use computer vision to determine the headset’s position and orientation. This approach requires no external hardware and is used by the Meta Quest 2, Quest 3, and HoloLens 2.
Advantages:

no external setup required
portable and flexible

Limitations:

can struggle in low-light or featureless environments
tracking volume limited by camera field of view

The mechanism underneath is worth naming now because Week 7 returns to it in detail. Inside-out tracking is a form of SLAM — simultaneous localisation and mapping. The device identifies visual features in the environment, builds a sparse map of them, and continuously estimates its own pose relative to that map. Two practical consequences follow.
The first is that tracking quality depends on the room. A space with plenty of visual texture — furniture, posters, patterned surfaces — tracks well. A blank white studio, a dark room, or a space dominated by reflective or repetitive surfaces tracks poorly, because the system cannot find or distinguish features. This is a common cause of “the headset is broken” reports that are actually room problems.
The second is drift. Small errors in pose estimation accumulate, so a virtual object left in place may be a few centimetres away from where it was after a period of use. Systems correct for this by recognising previously mapped areas, a process called relocalisation, which is also how content can be restored to the right place in a new session.


7.2 Outside-In Tracking
External sensors (base stations or cameras) track the headset and controllers. The HTC Vive Pro uses this approach with SteamVR base stations.
Advantages:

highly accurate and reliable
large tracking volume possible

Limitations:

requires setup and calibration
not portable

Outside-in tracking has largely lost the consumer market to inside-out, but it persists where precision matters more than convenience: motion capture, research settings, location-based entertainment and professional training installations. It also has a genuine technical advantage in that it does not depend on the visual texture of the room, and it does not suffer the same drift behaviour, since position is measured against fixed external references rather than an accumulated internal map.

8 The Hardware in This Module
You will have access to a range of devices throughout this module. Each offers different capabilities and design constraints. Week 2 examines this landscape comparatively; the purpose here is simply to know what is in the room.

8.1 Meta Quest 2
Standalone, 6DOF, inside-out tracking, touch controllers with haptics, and hand tracking. Still widely used in industry and education, and accepted for any session in this module that does not need colour passthrough.


8.2 Meta Quest 3
The primary target platform for this module. Adds full-colour passthrough for mixed reality, improved processing, and a slimmer form factor. Required rather than preferred from Week 7, where the mixed reality and scene understanding work depends on passthrough and room capture.


8.3 HTC Vive Pro
A PC-tethered headset with outside-in tracking via SteamVR base stations. Higher visual fidelity than the Quest 2. Useful for understanding the trade-offs between standalone and tethered systems.


8.4 Pico Neo Eye
Includes integrated eye tracking hardware. Enables gaze-based interaction and foveated rendering — relevant to the gaze input discussion in Week 4 and to the rendering techniques covered in Week 10.


8.5 HoloLens 2
Microsoft’s mixed reality headset. Optical see-through display, hand tracking, gaze tracking, voice input. The clearest available demonstration of the optical see-through constraints described above, and a useful comparison point for the spatial mapping work in Week 7.


8.6 Snap Spectacles 2022
Lightweight AR glasses with a small display. Useful for understanding the form factor trade-off between glasses and headsets, and available alongside Lens Studio as a platform option for Assessment 2.


8.7 Xreal One Pro AR Display Glasses
Lightweight tethered AR display glasses presenting a virtual screen without full world tracking. These present a virtual screen without tracking the world, which makes them a useful illustration of where “AR glasses” marketing outruns capability.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
9 Why XR Design is Different
Designing for XR requires a fundamentally different mindset from designing for screens.

9.1 The body is the interface
In XR, the user’s physical body — their hands, head, gaze, voice, and movement — becomes the primary input device. Design must account for physical ergonomics, fatigue, and the limits of human movement.
The practical implication is that interaction has a physical cost that accumulates. An interface element placed slightly too high is a minor annoyance on the first use and a source of genuine shoulder fatigue on the fiftieth. Screen interfaces do not degrade this way, and the habit of ignoring physical cost is one of the harder ones to unlearn. Week 4 gives this a name — gorilla arm — and a measurement method.


9.2 Space is the canvas
Rather than arranging elements on a flat surface, XR designers work in three-dimensional space. Objects have position, scale, and orientation. The user can move around them, look at them from different angles, and interact with them physically.
You also lose control of the camera. In film and in most games, the designer decides what the viewer sees and when; in XR, the user decides, and taking that control back is one of the most reliable ways to make someone unwell. Everything you might have done with a cut or a camera move must instead be done with composition, light, sound and motion. Week 8 is largely about the techniques that replace the camera.


9.3 Presence changes behaviour
Research has shown that people behave differently in immersive environments than they do in front of screens. They respond emotionally to virtual stimuli, feel genuine discomfort in threatening virtual situations, and can develop real skills through virtual practice. This makes XR a powerful tool — and a significant ethical responsibility.
The same mechanism that makes immersive training effective makes immersive persuasion effective, and the user has fewer defences than they do against a screen: they cannot easily look away, the content surrounds them, and the system knows where they are looking. Week 12 addresses this directly, but it is worth holding in mind from the first prototype rather than treating ethics as a topic that arrives near the end of term.


9.4 Comfort is a design constraint
Unlike screen-based interfaces, XR can cause physical discomfort — motion sickness, eye strain, neck fatigue, and disorientation. Good XR design treats comfort as a first-class design requirement, not an afterthought.
Two specific mechanisms are worth naming now. Vergence-accommodation conflict arises because your eyes converge on a virtual object at its apparent distance while remaining focused on the physical display a few centimetres away; the mismatch contributes to eye strain, particularly for near content. Frame timing matters because a dropped frame delays the world’s response to head movement, producing exactly the sensory conflict that causes nausea. Both are covered properly later — Week 3 for the perceptual account, Week 10 for the engineering — but note that comfort is where the perceptual and technical halves of this module meet, and that a comfort failure is not a polish issue you can defer.

This is a third-year module. You are expected to bring critical thinking, not just technical skill. Throughout the module, you will be asked to:

analyse existing XR experiences, not just build new ones

consider the ethical implications of immersive design

Concretely, the semester runs as two parallel tracks. The weekly lecture builds the conceptual and analytical vocabulary — what presence is, how perception works, which frameworks let you say precisely why an interaction fails. The practical and laboratory sessions extend your Unity competence on the hardware. The two are deliberately coupled: the concept introduced on the Monday is generally the thing you build or measure later in the week.
The assessment structure follows the same logic. Assessment 1 runs continuously and rewards evidenced practical work. Assessment 2, at the midpoint, asks you to look outward at an existing experience and deconstruct it, then prove the analysis by rebuilding one of its interactions. Assessment 3 is your own project, where you set the concept and defend the decisions. A recurring theme in the marking criteria is that a design choice you can justify is worth more than a technically impressive one you cannot.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
3 Standalone VR: Meta Quest 3 / 3S
The Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S represent the current mainstream of standalone VR — headsets with all compute, battery, and sensors onboard, requiring no PC or console tether.

3.1 Optics

The Quest 3 uses pancake lenses, which fold light path through polarisation to produce a thinner, sharper optical stack with less distortion at the edges.
The Quest 3S uses more traditional Fresnel lenses, which are cheaper to manufacture but introduce more “god rays” (visible light scatter) and a bulkier form factor.

This is a useful first lesson in hardware critique: two devices from the same manufacturer, released in the same product generation, can make very different optical trade-offs to hit different price points.
It is worth understanding why these two lens types behave differently, because the same physics recurs across every device in this module.
A Fresnel lens approximates a thick convex lens by collapsing it into concentric ridges. This makes it light and cheap, but each ridge boundary is a discontinuity that scatters light. When a bright object sits on a dark background — white text on black, a moon in a night sky — that scatter appears as radial streaks, the “god rays” users complain about. Fresnel lenses also have a small sweet spot: the image is sharp near the optical centre and degrades toward the edges, which is why users are told to adjust the fit until the image “clicks” into focus.
A pancake lens instead folds the light path back on itself two or three times inside a thin stack, using polarisation to control which pass exits toward the eye. The optical path length is preserved while the physical depth is not, which is what allows a thinner headset with a much larger sweet spot and far less edge distortion. The cost is light: each fold discards a large proportion of the light — typically most of it — so pancake optics require a substantially brighter and more power-hungry display to reach the same perceived brightness. Pancake optics are therefore a choice that spends battery and cost to buy comfort and clarity.
The lesson generalises. Optical designs in XR are not ranked from worse to better; they are trades between clarity, weight, brightness, power and price, and a manufacturer’s choice tells you which of those they prioritised for that product.


3.2 Passthrough and sensing
Both devices offer full-colour passthrough — external cameras feed a live video composite of the real world to the internal displays — plus depth sensing that allows virtual objects to be occluded correctly by real furniture and walls. This is what allows the Quest 3 family to market itself as “mixed reality” capable, not purely VR.
Passthrough is harder than it sounds, and understanding why explains most of its visible shortcomings.
The cameras are not where your eyes are. They sit on the front of the headset, several centimetres forward and apart from your actual eye positions, so the raw camera image has the wrong viewpoint. The system must reproject that image to your eyes’ perspective, which requires depth information — and where depth is wrong or missing, you get the warping around hands and door frames that users notice immediately.
Everything in the pipeline costs time. Capture, reprojection, composition and display each add latency, and the real world is now subject to that budget. A small delay between moving your head and the room responding is tolerable; a large one is nauseating, for exactly the reasons covered in Week 3.
Camera sensors also have far less dynamic range than the eye. A room with a bright window will show either a blown-out window or a dark interior, rarely both, and low-light performance is noticeably grainy. When you evaluate passthrough quality in the lab, look specifically at high-contrast scenes and at your own hands — those are where the pipeline shows its limits.


3.3 Input

Inside-out tracked controllers (retaining physical buttons, triggers, and haptics)
Camera-based hand tracking (no controllers required, lower fidelity, no haptic feedback)

Controllers are tracked by the same headset cameras that track the world, which has one important consequence: a controller the cameras cannot see is not tracked visually. Behind your back, close to your chest, or held against your body, the system falls back on the controller’s inertial sensors, which drift within about a second. This is why designers avoid interactions that require reaching behind the body, and why the Week 5 wrist menu sits where the cameras can see it.






NoteWhy this matters



Standalone hardware removed the PC-tether barrier that constrained the first consumer VR wave (2016). This is arguably the single biggest driver of mass XR adoption to date — cost, setup complexity, and physical tethering were the primary barriers identified in early VR adoption research.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
4 Mixed Reality Headsets

4.1 Apple Vision Pro
Apple explicitly avoids calling the Vision Pro a VR or AR headset — it is marketed as a “spatial computing” device. This is a deliberate positioning choice, not just a technical one.
Key characteristics:

visionOS introduces a new interaction paradigm built around windows, volumes, and spaces — 2D app windows, 3D volumetric content, and fully immersive environments can coexist
Eye tracking + pinch gesture input replaces controllers as the primary interaction model — you look at what you want and pinch to select
Uses passthrough (video see-through), not optical see-through, despite the “spatial computing” framing

The eye-tracking-plus-pinch model deserves attention because it is the clearest current answer to a problem we return to in Week 4: gaze is fast and effortless for pointing, but terrible for selecting, because we look at things constantly without meaning to act on them. Separating the two channels — eyes to indicate, hand to commit — sidesteps that. It also has a privacy dimension that Apple treats seriously: where a user looked is not reported to the application, only what they selected, because gaze data reveals attention, interest and arousal in ways users have no intuition about. We return to that in Week 12.


4.2 HoloLens 2
Microsoft’s HoloLens 2 takes a different technical approach entirely:

Optical see-through waveguide display — the user looks directly through a transparent lens with light guided into the eye, meaning the real world is never digitised or delayed
Narrower field of view than consumer VR headsets, a direct consequence of waveguide optics
Strong hand tracking and eye/gaze tracking, voice input
Positioned squarely for enterprise and industrial use cases (remote assistance, training, field service) rather than consumer entertainment

A waveguide works by injecting an image into the edge of a transparent pane, bouncing it along by total internal reflection, and extracting it toward the eye with a diffraction grating. The real world passes straight through the glass, which is why there is no latency and no camera pipeline. The costs are structural rather than incidental: gratings are wavelength-dependent, so colour uniformity is difficult; only a fraction of the injected light reaches the eye, so the display must be bright and the image still washes out in daylight; and the field of view is limited by the physics of the extraction optics rather than by cost. This is why optical see-through devices have narrow fields of view and are unlikely to catch up with headsets in that respect soon.
The consequence for you as a designer is the one raised in Week 1: additive light cannot produce black. On HoloLens, dark UI is invisible, drop shadows do nothing, and a “dimmed” background does not dim. Content has to be designed as luminous, high-contrast, and sparse.


4.3 Passthrough vs Optical See-Through
This is one of the most important technical distinctions in the whole module, because it explains many downstream differences in latency, fidelity, and use case.









Passthrough (Video See-Through)
Optical See-Through




How it works
Cameras capture the real world; a composite image is rendered and displayed on internal screens
A transparent lens/waveguide overlays digital content directly onto the user’s natural view


Examples
Quest 3, Vision Pro
HoloLens 2


Real-world fidelity
Limited by camera resolution, dynamic range, and field of view
Perfect — the user sees real, direct light


Latency risk
Camera-to-display lag can cause a subtle disconnect between real and virtual
None for the real-world view; only virtual content can lag


Occlusion of virtual content
Straightforward (composited digitally)
Harder — virtual light is added on top of real light, so true occlusion of virtual-behind-real is difficult



Two further consequences follow from the table and are worth stating explicitly.
Safety and failure behaviour differ. If an optical see-through device loses power or crashes, the user is looking through clear glass and can walk away. If a passthrough device does the same, the user is blind until they lift the headset. This matters for any application in a workplace, near machinery, or with vulnerable users.
Social visibility differs. Optical devices generally let others see the wearer’s eyes. Passthrough devices do not, which is why Vision Pro renders a synthetic image of the wearer’s eyes on an external display — an expensive engineering solution to a purely social problem, and a good illustration that hardware decisions in this field are frequently about acceptability rather than capability.

title: Lecture Notes
section: 5 AR Glasses: Xreal One Pro and Peers
text:
5 AR Glasses: Xreal One Pro and Peers
A third hardware category sits apart from headsets altogether: lightweight, glasses-form-factor AR devices such as the Xreal One Pro.
Characteristics:

Designed to look and feel like ordinary glasses — lightweight, low profile, socially acceptable to wear in public
Typically tethered to a phone, laptop, or dedicated puck for compute and battery
Use birdbath or waveguide optics to project a floating virtual screen in the user’s field of view — commonly used as a private, portable second monitor
Some newer models add spatial/positional tracking so content can be anchored to the room rather than simply following the user’s head
Optimised for portability and casual, short-duration wear — not for deep immersion or spatial interaction

Birdbath optics are worth distinguishing from waveguides, since both appear in this category. A birdbath design reflects the display off a beamsplitter into a curved mirror and back to the eye. It gives better colour and contrast than a waveguide at much lower cost, which is why media-viewing glasses use it — but the optical stack is bulkier and the transparency of the real world is reduced, so these devices look more like tinted sunglasses than clear lenses.
The critical question to ask of any device in this category is whether it tracks the world at all. Many “AR glasses” are 3DOF display devices: they show a screen that follows your head, with no knowledge of the room. That is a legitimate product — a private monitor is useful — but it is not augmented reality in the sense Azuma defined it, which requires registration in three dimensions (Azuma 1997). When you evaluate these in the lab, establish first whether content stays put when you walk around it.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
6 The Numbers That Actually Matter
Specification sheets are written to sell devices, and the most prominent numbers are frequently the least informative. Three in particular are worth being able to interpret.

6.1 Resolution, and why it misleads
A headset advertised at “4K per eye” sounds directly comparable to a 4K television, and is not. On a television, those pixels are spread across a screen occupying perhaps 30 degrees of your vision. In a headset, they are spread across 100 degrees or more. The same pixel count is stretched over three times the angular area, so the perceived sharpness is far lower than the number suggests.
The meaningful metric is pixels per degree (PPD) — how many pixels fall within one degree of your visual field. Current consumer headsets sit around 20–35 PPD. Human foveal vision resolves roughly 60 PPD, which is the informal target for “retinal” quality and which no consumer headset has yet reached. When comparing two devices, PPD tells you which will look sharper; raw resolution alone does not, because it says nothing about how widely those pixels are spread.
Low PPD produces the screen-door effect, where the unlit gaps between pixels become visible as a fine grid. It has largely receded on current hardware but is still noticeable on bright, uniform surfaces.


6.2 Field of view, and why quoted figures disagree
FOV can be quoted horizontally, vertically, or diagonally, and manufacturers naturally quote whichever is largest — usually the diagonal. Two devices claiming “110 degrees” may differ substantially in the horizontal figure that actually determines how much of a scene you see without turning your head.
There is also binocular overlap — the portion of the field both eyes see, which is where stereoscopic depth is available. A wide total FOV with poor overlap gives peripheral awareness but a narrower region of genuine depth perception.
For AR specifically, FOV is the dominant complaint about optical see-through devices, and it is a physics constraint rather than a cost one. Content that extends beyond the display simply stops at a hard edge, which is far more noticeable than a peripheral limit in VR because the real world continues around it.


6.3 Refresh rate
Quoted in hertz — commonly 72, 90 or 120. This is not a smoothness preference as it would be on a monitor; it sets the ceiling on motion-to-photon latency, the delay between moving your head and the display responding. Below roughly 20 milliseconds, most users are comfortable; above it, discomfort rises quickly.
The number on the box is the display’s capability. Whether your application actually achieves it is a separate question, and the subject of Week 10.


6.4 Panel technology

LCD — cheaper, good brightness and pixel fill, but weaker blacks and contrast. Used in the Quest series.
OLED / micro-OLED — true blacks, high contrast, very fast response; more expensive, and micro-OLED enables the small, dense panels that pancake optics and high PPD require. Used in Vision Pro.

Panel choice interacts with optics: pancake lenses discard most of the light, so they pair naturally with the brightness available from micro-OLED.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
7 Compute, Thermals, and Battery
A standalone headset is a mobile device. It runs a phone-class system-on-chip, rendering two views of your scene, every frame, while simultaneously running computer vision for tracking, hand detection and passthrough. That workload is substantial before your application does anything at all.
Three consequences follow, and all three will affect your Assessment 3 project.
Your frame budget is small. At 72Hz you have under 14 milliseconds per frame for everything, and the system has already spent part of it. This is why Week 10 treats performance as a comfort requirement rather than polish, and why techniques such as foveated rendering exist.
Thermal throttling is real. Sustained load heats the device, and the SoC reduces its clock speed to stay within thermal limits. A build that runs acceptably for five minutes may degrade noticeably after twenty. Test sessions long enough to see this, because your users will.
Battery constrains session design. Two to three hours is typical, less under heavy load. An experience intended for a classroom or exhibition has to account for charging, and for the fact that a warm headset is an uncomfortable one.
Tethered devices — the Vive Pro, or glasses tethered to a puck — trade mobility for a larger power and thermal envelope, which is precisely why they retain an advantage in visual fidelity. This is the same trade appearing again in a different form.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
8 Platform SDKs and App Stores
Hardware is only half the story. The software platform a device runs on determines what developers can build, how it is distributed, and how it is reviewed.

8.1 Meta Horizon OS

Built around the Meta XR SDK, with support for Unity, Unreal, and native development
Distribution via the Meta Horizon Store (curated, reviewed) and App Lab (lighter-touch, more experimental distribution)
Publishing requires meeting comfort ratings and performance benchmarks before an app can be listed

That last point is unusual and worth dwelling on. Meta will reject an application for failing to hold its frame rate. There are very few software platforms where performance is a review criterion rather than a quality preference — and the reason is the one established in Week 1, that a slow immersive application does not merely feel sluggish, it makes people unwell.


8.2 visionOS

Built around RealityKit and SwiftUI, developed almost exclusively through Xcode
Distribution via the Apple App Store, subject to Apple’s standard app review process
Apple publishes spatial-specific Human Interface Guidelines (HIG) that developers are expected to follow — covering topics like comfortable interaction distances, eye-tracking privacy, and window behaviour



8.3 OpenXR and the portability question
Both platforms above are vendor ecosystems, and building directly against either creates lock-in. OpenXR is the cross-vendor standard intended to address this: an application written against OpenXR can, in principle, run on any conformant runtime.
In practice, portability is partial. OpenXR covers the common core — sessions, spaces, input actions, rendering — but every vendor exposes distinguishing features through extensions, and those features are frequently the ones you actually want. Scene understanding, passthrough configuration and hand-tracking detail are typically vendor extensions. The realistic position is that OpenXR makes porting substantially cheaper, not free, and that is the assumption you should carry into a platform recommendation.
This is why your Unity projects in this module target OpenXR with the Meta feature group enabled: the standard underneath, the vendor’s capabilities on top.






ImportantConnecting back to Week 1



Your Week 1 practical PDP submission was the Meta Horizon OS pipeline in action — you experienced first-hand how an app moves from build to device via that ecosystem. This week’s practical asks you to research the visionOS pipeline and compare it directly against that experience.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
9 A Framework for Critical Comparison
Rather than memorising specification sheets, use these four criteria to evaluate any XR device you encounter — in this module, in industry, or in a device that has not been released yet:

Comfort — weight, weight distribution, fit, and how long a typical user can comfortably use it in one session
Field of view (FOV) — measured in degrees; affects edge clipping and how much of a task or environment is visible without turning the head
Tracking fidelity — the accuracy, latency, and robustness of head, hand, and/or eye tracking, especially in non-ideal conditions
Ecosystem maturity — the strength of the SDK, the size and quality of the app store or distribution channel, and the size of the developer and content community

These four criteria will recur throughout the module whenever we introduce a new device or platform.

9.1 Using the framework honestly
Two notes on applying it.
First, weight distribution matters more than weight. A heavier headset with a rear counterweight is frequently more comfortable over an hour than a lighter one that hangs entirely off the face. Total mass is the number on the spec sheet; the distribution is what the user feels. This is exactly the kind of judgement that only comes from wearing the device, which is what this week’s lab is for.
Second, tracking fidelity should be assessed under adverse conditions, not ideal ones. Every device tracks well in a well-lit, textured room while standing still. The differences appear in dim light, near blank walls, with fast head movement, or with a controller held out of camera view.


9.2 What the framework leaves out
No four-item framework is complete, and being able to say what yours omits is part of using it critically. Three candidates you may wish to add, depending on the brief:

Price and total cost of ownership — including controllers, facial interfaces, charging infrastructure and the replacement cost when a student drops one
Content and tooling availability — a technically superior device with no engine support and no content is not the better choice for a twelve-week project
Social acceptability and privacy — whether the device can reasonably be worn in front of other people, and what it records about the wearer and the room while doing so

The fourth criterion, ecosystem maturity, partly captures the second of these, but the framework as stated has nothing to say about cost or privacy — and in a real client recommendation, cost usually decides.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
10 Reading a Spec Sheet Critically
A short checklist you can apply to any device announcement:

Is the resolution given with a field of view? Without both, you cannot compute PPD, and the resolution figure alone tells you little.
Is the FOV horizontal or diagonal? If unstated, assume diagonal, which is the more flattering figure.
Is the refresh rate the display’s maximum or a sustained figure? These are different claims.
Is tracking 6DOF for the headset only, or for the controllers too?
Does it understand the room, or only show it? Passthrough is not scene understanding.
What is the battery figure measured doing? Idle, video playback and interactive rendering give very different numbers.
What is missing entirely? Weight distribution, thermal behaviour under sustained load, and daylight legibility are rarely in the marketing material and frequently decide whether a device is usable.

title: Lecture Notes
text:
11 Key Questions to Carry Forward

Is “spatial computing” a genuinely distinct technical category, or primarily a marketing category used to differentiate Apple’s device?
Does the “best” device for a given use case have to be the most technically impressive one?
How much should ecosystem maturity weigh against raw hardware specifications when recommending a platform to a client or employer?
If optical see-through cannot render black and cannot match a headset’s field of view, what class of applications is it nonetheless the right choice for?

Keep these questions in mind for this week’s lab and practical — you will be asked to take a position and justify it.

15 Summary

Standalone VR (Quest 3/3S), MR headsets (Vision Pro, HoloLens 2), and AR glasses (Xreal One Pro) represent three genuinely distinct hardware philosophies, not just different price points of the same idea
Optical designs — Fresnel, pancake, waveguide, birdbath — are trades between clarity, weight, brightness, power and cost, not a ranking from worse to better
Passthrough vs optical see-through is a key technical and experiential distinction with knock-on effects for latency, fidelity, occlusion, safety and social visibility

Comfort, FOV, tracking fidelity, and ecosystem maturity together form a repeatable, transferable framework for critiquing any XR device — provided you can also say what it leaves out

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Why perception matters


XR works by deceiving the perceptual system.
To design effective XR experiences, you need to understand:

how the brain constructs the experience of being somewhere
what cues it relies on
what happens when those cues conflict



The brain fuses multiple sensory streams into one perceived reality.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Presence


Presence is the subjective feeling of being in a place.
Slater (2009) distinguishes two components:

Place illusion: the sense of being in the virtual place
Plausibility illusion: the sense that what is happening is real



Presence emerges from the overlap of place illusion and plausibility illusion.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Place Illusion


The feeling that you are actually in the virtual environment.
Supported by:

wide field of view
head tracking
spatial audio
physical scale

Broken by:

tracking errors
low frame rate
visible display edges



A wide, stable field of view is central to sustaining place illusion.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Plausibility Illusion


The feeling that the events in the virtual environment are really happening.
Supported by:

responsive virtual agents
consistent physics
cause and effect relationships

Broken by:

objects passing through each other
unresponsive environments
implausible events



Consistent, responsive events sustain the plausibility illusion.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Immersion vs Presence


These are often confused but are distinct concepts.
Immersion is an objective property of the technology.

how much of the sensory field does the system replace?
how accurately does it track movement?

Presence is a subjective psychological response.

how much does the user feel they are there?

High immersion tends to support presence but does not guarantee it.


Immersion is measured in hardware; presence is felt by the user.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
The Reality Trade-off


More immersion is not always better.
Trade-offs include:

comfort vs presence
cost vs quality
portability vs fidelity

Design for the right level of immersion for the task.


Every gain in fidelity is weighed against cost, comfort and portability.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Perceptual Modalities


The brain integrates information from multiple sensory systems.
In XR, the most relevant are:

visual
auditory
proprioceptive
vestibular
haptic



Five perceptual channels feed into the brain’s single model of reality.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Visual Perception


The dominant sense in most XR systems.
Key factors:

stereopsis (depth from two eyes)
motion parallax (depth from movement)
accommodation and vergence
peripheral vision



Stereopsis: two slightly different retinal images are fused into depth.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Auditory Perception


Spatial audio contributes significantly to presence.
The brain uses:

interaural time difference (ITD)
interaural level difference (ILD)
spectral cues from the ear shape (HRTF)

Mismatched audio breaks presence rapidly.


Timing and level differences between the ears let us localise sound in space.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Proprioception


The sense of the position and movement of your own body.
In VR, proprioception can conflict with visual information.
Example: your body feels stationary but your visual system sees movement.
This conflict is a primary cause of simulator sickness.


A mismatch between felt body position and seen motion creates sensory conflict.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Vestibular System


The inner ear detects:

linear acceleration
rotational acceleration
gravity

In VR, visual motion without vestibular motion creates conflict.
This is the main cause of vection-induced sickness.


The vestibular system reports no motion while the eyes report movement.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Haptic Perception


The sense of touch and force.
Current XR systems provide limited haptic feedback.
The absence of haptic feedback is a significant limitation for:

object manipulation
surface interaction
social presence



Vibration alone stands in for the rich forces of real touch.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Proximal and Distal Stimuli


Distal stimulus: the actual object or event in the world
Proximal stimulus: the pattern of energy that reaches the sensory receptor
In XR, we manipulate the proximal stimulus to create the perception of a distal stimulus that does not exist.


XR recreates the proximal signal without the distal object ever existing.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Simulator Sickness


A form of motion sickness caused by sensory conflict in simulated environments.
Symptoms:

nausea
disorientation
eye strain
headache
fatigue



Sensory conflict during use can leave lasting symptoms after removal.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Causes of Simulator Sickness



Latency: delay between head movement and display update
Low frame rate: judder and motion blur
Vection: visual motion without vestibular motion
FOV mismatch: visual motion at the wrong scale
Vergence-accommodation conflict



Each contributing cause introduces a mismatch the brain must resolve.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Mitigation Strategies


Design choices that reduce simulator sickness:

maintain frame rate above 72Hz
minimise motion-to-photon latency (below 20ms)
use teleportation instead of smooth locomotion
add vignette during movement
allow users to choose comfort settings
provide rest breaks



A vignette narrows the field of view during motion to reduce visual conflict.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Health Effects


Beyond simulator sickness, extended XR use can cause:

eye strain and fatigue
neck and shoulder strain
disorientation after removal
social isolation



Extended sessions place cumulative strain on the eyes, neck and shoulders.

title: Lecture Slides
text:
Ethical Considerations


XR designers have a responsibility to:

disclose health risks
provide comfort options
design for accessibility
avoid exploiting presence for manipulation



Designing responsibly means weighing persuasive power against user wellbeing.

Discussion

Can Place Illusion exist without Plausibility Illusion, or vice versa? Can you think of an experience that demonstrates one without the other?
Is chasing ever-higher immersion always a sound design goal, given diminishing returns and increased risk of simulator sickness?
Where should the line be drawn between using presence to create beneficial experiences (e.g. therapy, training) and using it to manipulate (e.g. advertising, persuasive design)?
Should XR platforms be required to disclose health risks before use, similar to warnings on medical devices or pharmaceuticals?
Given that susceptibility to simulator sickness varies widely between individuals, how might this affect who can fully participate in XR experiences — and what should designers do about it?


Good prompts for small-group discussion or an after-class reflective post. Encourage students to connect answers back to Slater’s PI/Psi model.
